opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I read quite a lot into it, maybe more than I should have. When the upperclassman listed them as Professor Jun Zhu first, then Professor Jie Tang, then Professor Peng Cui, my instinct was that this was a kind of ranking: the first name was the one they thought fit me best, or the one they'd go to themselves. As an undergrad you don't have much information. You're just looking for any signal you can get, so the order of a list feels meaningful.

Looking back, I think it was partly that and partly just how it came out in conversation. Professor Zhu's group was doing machine learning, Bayesian methods and later a lot of deep learning and reinforcement learning, and that was closest to what I was curious about. So it made sense that it came up first for someone with my interests. Professor Tang's lab was strong in data mining and knowledge graphs, and Professor Cui's in network and data-driven research. Those are all great groups, just different directions.

So I took the order as a hint, not a verdict. It nudged me to reach out to Professor Zhu's lab first, and that ended up shaping a lot of what came after. The bigger lesson for me was that the people a year or two ahead of you are incredibly valuable. Even a casual "you should talk to these people, in this order" can change your path more than you expect.

r001.rationale: The response says Weng read the order as a ranking of personal fit or preference, not as a ranking of how impressive the labs were.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't read too much into it. The upperclassman just listed them in a row, Jun Zhu, Jie Tang, Peng Cui, and I took that as a ranked order of how strongly he recommended each one, probably based on how well he thought they matched what I wanted to do. Jun Zhu's group was very focused on machine learning fundamentals, Bayesian methods, generative models, so that came first because I had said I wanted to do machine learning. Jie Tang's lab was more about data mining and social networks, and Peng Cui's was somewhere in between.

Looking back, I think the order said more about him than about the labs. Those were the people he had direct contact with, and his own experience shaped the list. I ended up talking to a few people and visiting, and it became clear that the "best lab" on paper isn't the point. What mattered was whether the day-to-day work excited me and whether I'd get real hands-on time rather than just doing chores for a senior PhD student. So I treated the list as a starting point for conversations, not a verdict.
